doc_summary: Podcast conversation on AI control: ensuring safety even if models are scheming, via red-team control evaluations, trusted monitoring, and protocols tested on a backdoor-insertion setting. Includes explicit assumptions about adversarial evaluation, model awareness of tests, and what evidence is convincing.

items.claim: prefers worst-case, assume-the-model-knows-it-is-tested control evaluations over behavioral evidence of apparent alignment because a scheming model could look good on purpose to cause problems later.
items.quote: no matter how your AI is behaving, you have to worry that it's just behaving that way because it thinks it has some way of looking good now in the hopes of causing problems later.

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence and adversarial training as proof of alignment, since a model that was caught and trained away may just be better at hiding or evading the training.
items.quote: it's not clear that you've necessarily made it aligned versus just made it better at hiding or better at avoiding adversarial training.

items.claim: prefers assuming the model recognizes it is in a red-team exercise over hoping it is naive, because evaluation validity must not depend on the model failing to notice the test.
items.quote: If you're trying to harness your untrusted AI during the red teaming, it might know that it's in a red teaming exercise. Buck Shlegeris: You always assume that it does.

items.claim: In a setup, model the real deployment architecture (scaffold, inference server, dev machine, ordinary agentic code-running loop) instead of an exotic or paranoid-looking contrived scenario, because realistic infrastructure makes the threat model concrete and mirrors actual use.
items.quote: I think this is a very realistic way for things to be set up. I'm not describing something which is particularly paranoid: this is probably how Code Interpreter works right now.

items.claim: Use sting operations that mix fake but realistic-looking dangerous items into the normal stream of real work to measure whether monitors actually catch them, instead of announcing tests.
items.quote: we're just constantly running sting operations, where some fraction of the queries you'll see are fake queries that you should report.

items.claim: prefers red teams that search for the best attack strategies over ones that imitate what an evil AI would psychologically plan, because security-style adversarial analysis should not rely on guessing the attacker's psychology.
items.quote: I'd prefer the red team to be less in the mindset of like, "What are the sort of plans an evil AI might think of," and more in the mindset of like, "What are the best plans that an AI could follow,"

items.claim: Elicit the model's strongest attack by giving it hidden reasoning, iterative ideation, and the ability to abstain on most tasks, rather than a bare prompt, since a naively prompted model underestimates its capability to behave adversarially.
items.quote: if you just prompt the model, it doesn't do that good of a job. But you can do something where first you ask it "okay, think of some ideas". And then we have it point out issues with those ideas and iterate

items.claim: Choose test tasks where the harmful action is embedded in work the model is genuinely expected to do (e.g., writing infrastructure code with subtle backdoors) rather than flagrantly dangerous affordances, since those are the realistic and costly-to-avoid failure channels.
items.quote: it's very easy to prevent the AI from launching the nukes, because you just don't give it access to the nukes... But on the other hand, it would be very costly to never use the AI to help you write infrastructure code.

items.claim: Avoid giveaway artifacts in malicious behavior: obviously contrived markers like magic numbers or primes are easily flagged, so plausible-looking edge-case handling is what counts as a realistic subtle failure.
items.quote: part of our overall prompting for the model is, does your idea involve inserting egregious magic numbers? If so, don't do that. That's going to get caught.

items.claim: Treat single-setting results as modest evidence only; claim the methodology and building blocks transfer rather than the specific numbers or protocol rankings.
items.quote: We're not saying that you should assume that the protocols that worked for us will work in future, though it does seem like it's some evidence, but you should follow the same kind of control evaluation methodology

items.claim: prefers an empirical per-domain measurement over intuition about whether checking is easier than generating, because answers depend on the specific domain and can be directly evaluated.
items.quote: this question is empirically evaluatable per domain, and our recommendation would be you empirically evaluate it per domain.

items.claim: Flags as an open research topic finding better evidence for why current models are not scheming than informal impressions of their answers.
items.quote: I wish that I had a better answer to this question and I think this is an important topic for future research.
